sources.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis I: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I (open textbook), Chapter 4 'The Derivative', version 6.3 (May 15, 2026)
sources.locator: Chapter 4, §4.1.1-§4.1.2 (Definition 4.1.1, Propositions 4.1.7 and 4.1.10, Exercise 4.1.3) and §4.2.1-§4.2.5 (Theorems 4.2.3, 4.2.4, 4.2.11 and Propositions 4.2.6-4.2.8), printed pp. 154-168 of the volume, read completely, with the proofs of Theorem 4.2.4 and Proposition 4.2.7 inspected line by line

contents.name: §4.1.1 Definition 4.1.1: the derivative f'(c) as the limit of the difference quotient at a limit point of the domain, and differentiability on a set
contents.support: The library's published definition def-derivative has exactly this limit-of-difference-quotient form at a limit point; the pair's items use the library form, and this source confirms the convention (interior and one-sided endpoint derivatives included).

contents.name: §4.1.2 Proposition 4.1.7 (Linearity): (alpha f)' = alpha f' and (f+g)' = f' + g' for differentiable real functions on an interval
contents.support: The pair's theorem differentiates the affine parameter path theta -> theta_0 + theta u componentwise; each scalar component theta -> (theta_0)_j + theta u_j is a sum of a constant and a scalar multiple of the identity, which is exactly the pair of rules stated here and carried by the published library form thm-algebra-of-derivatives.

contents.name: §4.1.2 Proposition 4.1.10 (Chain rule) for real functions of one variable: h = f o g differentiable with h'(c) = f'(g(c)) g'(c)
contents.support: The one-variable prototype of the chain rule used by the pair for the composite F o gamma; the pair consumes the published Euclidean total-derivative form thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives, whose scalar case this proposition corroborates.

contents.name: §4.1.3 Exercise 4.1.3: for every integer n the power x -> x^n is differentiable with the usual derivative (in particular the identity x -> x has derivative 1 and constants have derivative 0)
contents.support: The pair obtains the partial derivative of the affine component theta -> (theta_0)_j + theta u_j from the case n = 1 and from constants; the published library form is lem-derivative-of-a-power, whose n = 0 and n = 1 clauses are the ones used.

contents.name: §4.2.3 Theorem 4.2.4 (Mean value theorem): f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) gives f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b-a) for some c in (a,b), with its Rolle-based proof
contents.support: The deterministic bounded-error comparison consumed by the pair is proved by exactly this MVT applied on the interval between the candidate and the centre; the library form is cor-mean-value-theorem, whose hypotheses (continuity on the closed interval, differentiability on the interior) match the pair's use.

contents.name: §4.2.4 Propositions 4.2.6-4.2.8: f' = 0 implies f constant; f' >= 0 implies f nondecreasing and f' > 0 implies f strictly increasing, all proved from the mean value theorem
contents.support: The quantitative consequence used by the pair, |f(theta) - f(theta_0)| >= m|theta - theta_0| when f(theta_0) = 0 and f' >= m > 0, is the MVT application recorded in this proposition family; the library form is thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative, and this source confirms that no continuity of f' is needed for it.

contents.name: §4.2.5 Theorem 4.2.11 (Darboux): a derivative on an interval attains every value between two of its values
contents.support: Recorded because it lies inside the read section and confirms that sign constancy of a nonvanishing derivative needs no continuity hypothesis; the pair's own route uses the mean value theorem instead, and the published library form is thm-darboux-theorem-for-derivatives.

sources.title: G. L. Luke, Notes of lectures on Multivariable Calculus (University of Oxford course notes hosted at people.maths.ox.ac.uk/~tillmann), October 14, 2007
sources.locator: §1 Introduction (derivatives of curves and directional derivatives), §2 'The Total Derivative' (Definition 3, the relation between total and directional derivatives, the 'Beware' warning, the matrix representation and the gradient), §3 'Properties of Total Derivatives' (linearity and the Chain Rule Theorem 2 with proof), §7 'Mean Value Theorem' (Theorem 5, the scalar gradient form f(b)-f(a) = grad f(c)(b-a) with c on the segment, and Theorem 6); PDF pp. 1-3 and 5-6 and 9-13 read completely

contents.name: §2 Definition 3: the total derivative as the linear map L with f(a+Delta) - f(a) - L(Delta) = o(|Delta|), together with the first-order expansion and the remark that it is the best linear approximation
contents.support: The library's Euclidean total-derivative definition is exactly this first-order expansion with a normalized o(||h||_2) remainder; the notes' finite-dimensional setting (where the o-condition is norm-independent) matches the library convention used by the pair.

contents.name: §2 The paragraph 'What is the relationship between the total derivative and the directional derivatives?': if the total derivative exists then Df_a(v) equals the directional derivative of f at a in the direction v
contents.support: This is exactly the identity used by the pair to pass between the chain-rule derivative of the composite along the line and the Euclidean directional derivative D_uF; the library form thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives is cited for both directions of the identification.

contents.name: §2 'Beware': there are examples where the total derivative fails to exist at a point even though all directional derivatives exist; and §2 the worked existence example in the (Delta_1, Delta_2) plane
contents.reason: The pair imposes the C^1 hypothesis (continuous partial derivatives), under which total differentiability is guaranteed; the warning motivates the hypothesis choice but no item of this pair constructs or consumes a directional-without-total-differentiability example, and none of the pair's consumers needs one.

contents.name: §2 Definition 4 and the following paragraphs: the matrix of the total derivative with respect to chosen bases, the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives, and the gradient of a scalar map as the row of partial derivatives
contents.support: The pair reads the total derivative of the affine path off its Jacobian matrix and writes the hypothesis through the gradient of the scalar prediction; the library form def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient fixes exactly these conventions.

contents.name: §7 'Mean Value Theorem': the scalar case -- for f : U subset R^k -> R differentiable with a + t(b-a) in U, f(b) - f(a) = grad f(a + t_0(b-a)) . (b-a) = Df_{a+t_0(b-a)}(b-a) for some t_0 on the segment
contents.reason: This scalar gradient form is an equivalent alternative route to the pair's key inequality |F(theta)| >= m|theta|, but the pair's recorded U1 route proceeds through the one-variable bounded-error lemma and the chain rule, so no item of this pair consumes the gradient form and no planned page of this run needs it recorded as a built result.

contents.name: §7 Theorem 5 (one-variable mean value theorem) and Theorem 6: for C^1 f : U subset R^n -> R^m on a segment, ||f(b) - f(a)|| <= sup ||Df|| ||b-a|| (proved through g(t) = f(a + t(b-a)) and Cauchy-Schwarz)
contents.support: The vector-valued upper-bound companion of the pair's scalar lower bound; it records that no lower bound on the displacement is available from differentiability alone, which is why the pair carries the monotone response hypothesis. The library form thm-mean-value-inequality-for-total-derivatives is the total-derivative version of Theorem 6.

contents.name: §3 'Properties of Total Derivatives', items 1 and 2: the total derivative is linear at each point, and D(cf) = c Df, D(f+g) = Df + Dg
contents.support: The linearity of the total derivative used implicitly when reading D gamma as the map h -> hu and when composing with DF; the library form is thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives, whose statement is the same pair of rules for Euclidean domains.

contents.name: §3 'Properties of Total Derivatives', item 3: Chain Rule, Theorem 2 with proof -- D(g o f)_a = Dg_{f(a)} o Df_a on open domains with f(U_1) contained in U_2
contents.support: Exactly the tool the pair uses to differentiate the composite F o gamma; the notes' remainder-expansion proof is the classical argument, and the library form thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives is the cited statement.

contents.name: §5, §6, §8, §9 (inverse and implicit function theorems, Lagrange multipliers, submanifolds, appendices) and §4 (applications to the determinant and the inverse-function theorem)
contents.reason: These sections treat inverse/implicit-function, submanifold and constrained-optimisation material with no consumer among this pair's two items or the planned pages of this run; they were inspected only to identify the sections that carry the total-derivative and mean-value material above.

canonical.name: The pair's own result: uncertainty analysis for a C^1 prediction on a Euclidean configuration space along a declared unit direction, reduced to the recorded U1 bounded-error comparison (completed-expansion-arguments.md#U1) on the affine composite
canonical.support: Not a heading of either source: it is the pair's constructed theorem, which states that bounded-error data (|yhat| <= s, |y - yhat| <= delta, y = F(theta_0 + theta u)) confine the family parameter to |theta| <= (s+delta)/m under the gradient lower bound <grad F(theta_0+theta u), u> >= m > 0; the proof verifies the hypotheses of lem-em-bounded-error-model-comparison for the composite response and then applies that lemma. Sources A and B back the standard differential-calculus ingredients (chain rule, gradient/directional derivatives, mean value theorem).

canonical.name: The pair's own example: sharpness of the bound for the linear prediction F(theta) = m theta with yhat = 0, s = 0, and failure of any finite bound when the response lower bound is dropped
canonical.support: Not a heading of either source: it is the pair's constructed sharpness example, specialising the theorem to n = 1, u = 1 and F(theta) = m theta, where the compatible set is exactly |theta| <= delta/m with equality attained; the hypothesis-necessity part records that for F = 0 every parameter is compatible. Source A backs the derivative and absolute-value arithmetic used.
